studies.label: Food-waste brainstorming experiment: reanalysis of flexibility

counts_source.quote: The remaining 52 participants (age: mean=22.3, min=18, max=37 years old; gender: 8 female, 44 male) were university students enrolled mostly in informatics study programs.

arms.name: human+AI
arms.description: Individual brainstorming in a custom app with on-demand AI idea suggestions. Participants were asked to request suggestions at least once and could copy suggestions from a separate panel into their own idea list; only accepted suggestions counted toward their result. PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), sections 3.1–3.2; analyzed arm size: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), section 4.

arms.name: human-only
arms.description: Baseline individual brainstorming without AI idea suggestions. PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.1; analyzed arm size: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), section 4.

studies.task: Individually generate ideas answering ‘How can we reduce food waste?’ in the study’s brainstorming app.

ai_tool.name: OpenAI gpt-3.5-turbo-0301
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.2: the model is explicitly named; its release year is not stated in the paper.

preregistration.where: No preregistration is stated in the complete paper.

studies.shared_sample: The paper explicitly reuses data from an earlier study described only as under review, concerning human-AI brainstorming and idea quantity, novelty and value. Its bibliographic identity and candidate ID are not supplied. PDF p. 1 (printed p. 421), section 1; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.2. No particular later publication is assumed to share this sample.

estimates.outcome: Flexibility of the submitted idea list, including accepted AI ideas (H1)
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Number of distinct categories covered by each participant’s retained idea list using the predefined Specht and Buck food-waste category system. A student assistant blind to condition categorized the ideas; uncategorized and deleted ideas were excluded. Accepted/copied AI suggestions in the participant’s list count toward this outcome; other logged AI suggestions do not. PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), section 3.3, Table 1 and section 4.1; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), section 4.1.

sources.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to conditions and were equally distributed across conditions (human-only: 26, human+ai: 26).
The remaining 52 participants (age: mean=22.3, min=18, max=37 years old; gender: 8 female, 44 male) were university students enrolled mostly in informatics study programs.

sources.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), section 4.1, first paragraph
sources.quote: The test showed a significant difference (U=546.5, p<.001) between the human+AI condition (mdn=5) and the human-only condition (mdn=2), with a strong effect size (rank-biserial correlation rB=.617).

estimates.notes: The quoted medians are human+AI=5 and human-only=2; they are not entered as means. The paper’s effect is specifically a rank-biserial correlation (rB), not a standardized mean difference. The Mann-Whitney test compares one category count per participant. Although the paper calls this team-level diversity, each team contains one human and the AI, and the score measures breadth within that human’s submitted list. A single category-coverage mean is printed without arm attribution and is not used as an arm mean. Arm means, SDs, SEs and confidence intervals are not printed; no values were read from the boxplot. H1 is a main hypothesis, but no preregistration is stated. The rank-biserial correlation is coded paper_effect.type=other to retain its specific identity; it is not relabeled as a Pearson correlation or converted into a standardized mean difference. No standardizing divisor is stated, so standardizer remains null.

estimates.outcome: Flexibility of human-authored ideas, excluding AI-origin ideas (H2)
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Number of distinct categories among each participant’s human-authored retained ideas, excluding AI-origin ideas in the human+AI condition. Uses the same predefined category system and condition-blind coding as the submitted-list outcome. PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), section 3.3; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), section 4.1, second-hypothesis paragraph.

sources.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to conditions and were equally distributed across conditions (human-only: 26, human+ai: 26).
The remaining 52 participants (age: mean=22.3, min=18, max=37 years old; gender: 8 female, 44 male) were university students enrolled mostly in informatics study programs.

sources.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), section 4.1, second-hypothesis paragraph
sources.quote: We found no significant difference between the two conditions (U=326.0, p=.830).

estimates.notes: The Mann-Whitney test compares one category count per participant. Human-authored ideas were produced while AI suggestions were available, so this is with_ai, not an unassisted follow-up. Arm means, SDs, SEs, confidence intervals and a treatment effect size are not printed. A single category-coverage mean is printed without arm attribution and is not used as an arm mean. Arm medians and other values shown only in the boxplot are not estimated from the figure. H2 is a main hypothesis, but no preregistration is stated. The printed p-value precision is retained in the source quotation (p=.830).

estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: For each participant, average number of human-authored ideas per category covered; the paper assigns zero to participants with no ideas. Higher values mean more human ideas within each covered category. This is depth within a participant’s ideas, not diversity across participants. PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), section 4.1, final paragraph before section 4.2.

sources.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to conditions and were equally distributed across conditions (human-only: 26, human+ai: 26).
The remaining 52 participants (age: mean=22.3, min=18, max=37 years old; gender: 8 female, 44 male) were university students enrolled mostly in informatics study programs.

sources.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), section 4.1, final paragraph before section 4.2
sources.quote: shows a significant difference (U=119.0, p<.001) in the average number of ideas per category between human-only (mdn=2) and human+ai (mdn=1) condition.

estimates.notes: The quoted medians are human+AI=1 and human-only=2; they are not entered as means. The Mann-Whitney test uses one within-category fluency value per participant. No arm means, SDs, SEs, confidence intervals or effect size are printed. The outcome averages ideas within covered categories; higher_is=more_ideas refers to that within-category rate and does not assert that greater concentration in fewer categories is greater flexibility.

estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Participant mean number of retained human-origin ideas, excluding AI-origin suggestions, from the human column of Table 2. These are per-person means rather than the condition-level totals of logged human and AI ideas. PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Table 2 and section 3.3.

sources.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to conditions and were equally distributed across conditions (human-only: 26, human+ai: 26).
The remaining 52 participants (age: mean=22.3, min=18, max=37 years old; gender: 8 female, 44 male) were university students enrolled mostly in informatics study programs.

sources.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Table 2, human+AI and human-only rows; columns AI, human, Total

estimates.notes: Use the human-origin column, not the AI-origin column or total logged corpus. Table 2 reports these arm means but no SDs, SEs, interval, numerical treatment test or effect size. Section 4.1 says human-only participants contributed significantly more human ideas (PDF p. 6, printed p. 426); section 5.1 instead says no significant difference was observed in human idea number (PDF p. 8, printed p. 428). The significance discrepancy is unresolved, so no p-value or test statistic is inferred.

estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Number of ideas produced jointly by a human and the AI compared with a human working alone, reported only in the discussion. The passage does not identify whether this quantity includes only accepted AI suggestions or all logged suggestions, and it does not state the analysis unit. PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), section 5.1; participation and idea-list procedure: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.1.

sources.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to conditions and were equally distributed across conditions (human-only: 26, human+ai: 26).
The remaining 52 participants (age: mean=22.3, min=18, max=37 years old; gender: 8 female, 44 male) were university students enrolled mostly in informatics study programs.

sources.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), section 5.1, final paragraph beginning "For our setting"
sources.quote: For our setting, we find that the human working with the AI jointly produced significantly more ideas as compared to alone.

estimates.notes: The authors report that joint human-AI idea quantity was significantly greater than human-only idea quantity. No numerical test, p-value or significance threshold, effect size, arm means, SDs, SEs or confidence intervals are supplied for this joint-output comparison; all statistics remain null. The discussion does not state the analysis unit, so unit remains null. The participant counts are the printed analyzed sample in section 4; no separate sample is specified for this claim. The S1-O5 link refers only to the separate joint-quantity narrative retained in that screening entry, not to its full logged corpus. Section 3.1 says unaccepted AI suggestions do not count toward participants’ results, whereas Table 2 includes such suggestions; section 5.1 does not explicitly resolve which idea set supports the claim. Accordingly, no Table 2 totals or means are assigned to this contrast, and no combined quantity, mean, p-value or effect is calculated. The accepted-versus-logged definition remains an open item. This comparison concerns output produced with AI available, not an unassisted follow-up. It is distinct from the human-authored idea-count outcome.

not_extracted.what: S1-O5: Total logged idea quantity, including all retained AI suggestions
not_extracted.reason: The Table 2 corpus includes unaccepted AI suggestions, which section 3.1 explicitly excludes from participants’ submitted results. These logged totals are not a scored participant-output fluency outcome. The separate section 5.1 narrative comparison of joint human-AI idea quantity is retained as s1_joint_idea_fluency_human_ai_vs_human_only, with statistics and analysis unit left null. Its accepted-versus-logged idea set is unresolved, so Table 2 values are not assigned to that contrast. PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.1; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Table 2 and section 4.1; PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), section 4.1; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), section 5.1.

not_extracted.reason: Descriptive comparison of AI-origin suggestions with human-origin ideas pooled across randomized conditions. PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), section 4.2; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), Figure 5 and accompanying text. Percentages shown only in the figure are not transcribed.

not_extracted.reason: Descriptive source/process comparison within human+AI sessions only; AI versus human contributions are not randomized participant arms or AI configurations. PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), section 4.2.

not_extracted.reason: Open-ended self-reports about participants’ experiences rather than creativity or diversity scores on their output. PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), section 4.3.

not_extracted.what: Association between human-authored idea quantity and number of categories covered
not_extracted.reason: The reported Spearman correlation is an association between two output measures, not an effect of randomized AI assistance. PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), section 4.1.

not_extracted.what: Novelty and value of individual ideas in the earlier under-review study
not_extracted.reason: The introduction identifies these as outcomes of an earlier report whose data were reused; the present paper does not report their arm statistics or numerical contrasts. The other study is not bibliographically identified. PDF p. 1 (printed p. 421), section 1; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.2.

not_extracted.what: Frequency of requests for AI suggestions
not_extracted.reason: This is tool-use activity within the assisted condition, not a score on creative output or an assigned-arm comparison. PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), section 4: “Participants in the human+ai condition requested AI input 148 times (mean=5.7), but only a subset of these ideas is reflected in the final idea set.”.

open_items: Arm-specific participant-level means, SDs, SEs and confidence intervals for the two flexibility outcomes and within-category fluency are not printed. Human-authored idea count has arm means but no SDs, SEs or numerical contrast test. No standardized mean differences or uncertainty are derived from the rank tests, medians, figures or rank-biserial correlation. PDF pp. 5–6 (printed pp. 425–426), sections 4–4.1 and Table 2.

The total and per-arm randomized counts are not explicit, nor are the excluded participants’ arms or the timing of exclusions relative to randomization. Retain only the printed analyzed counts. PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), section 4.

Identify the earlier under-review report to settle sample overlap; the present paper confirms reuse but gives no full citation. PDF p. 1 (printed p. 421), section 1; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.2.

Resolve the conflicting significance claims about human-origin idea counts in section 4.1 and section 5.1. No numerical test is printed to resolve them. PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426) and PDF p. 8 (printed p. 428).

Clarify the accepted-versus-logged idea set and underlying statistics behind the joint-quantity claim in section 5.1. Table 2’s logged corpus cannot substitute for participant-submitted output. PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Table 2; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), section 5.1.

The country of data collection is not explicitly named; the methods describe students attending a Western European university. The model release year is also not printed. Country and model year are not inferred from affiliations or the model name. PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), section 3.3; PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.2.
